Decision support for hazmat response
hazbrief

A truck or a rail car is leaking something dangerous.
We give the commander the whole picture in minutes.

Real-time decision support for emergency response to hazardous material releases on highways and rail lines.

Problem statement

The first hour decides the outcome.
Today's tools are too slow for it.

  • When a hazardous material gets loose, every minute counts: protect people, send help, limit the loss of life and property.
  • The tools that model the danger are locked away and take special training to run.
  • Someone gathers the data, runs the old tools, and pastes the results into a briefing by hand.
  • What comes out is static: not interactive, and not flexible enough to deal with change quickly.
The commander needs an answer good enough to act on, while there is still time to act.

146

$209.5M
in damage to rail equipment and track alone from those 146
Each circle is one of the 146 rail accidents; a bigger circle means more reported damage. Sources: Bureau of Transportation Statistics; Federal Railroad Administration accident reports.

Solution overview

Tell it what happened. Get the whole picture back.

In: where, what, when.
Typed or spoken. No software training.
➜
Out: the danger area on a live map, who and what is inside it, the responders nearby, the first actions, and a draft briefing. A workup in 3 or 4 minutes.
hazbrief4
Solution overview · the gas over time

It shows where the gas will be, and when.

15 minutes after the release
1 hour 15 minutes after the release

Red is life-threatening, orange is serious harm, yellow is discomfort. The cloud follows the forecast wind, hour by hour, so a commander can see which road, school or neighborhood it reaches next.

hazbrief5
Solution overview · why this is new
No one has a tool like this.

The pieces exist: the guidebook distances, the gas models, the population counts, the briefing form. We are the first to put them together, live, in one place, for deciding quickly with data when every minute counts.

hazbrief7
Solution overview · the person stays in charge

It keeps the expert's brain switched on.

  • Every picture opens with a checklist of what to verify before acting.
  • It says what is assumed, what is modelled, and what data is missing.
  • The expert checks it against what they see at the scene and what they know.
  • We do the assembly. The person makes the call.
hazbrief8
Solution overview · the briefing, at once

The briefing is drafted the moment the picture is.

  • The standard incident briefing form (ICS 201), filled in block by block.
  • Every line names where it came from.
  • Built from the data gathered for this incident, at this place and hour.
  • A draft for the commander to review, correct and sign.

Technical approach

One server. Seven tools. Many public sources at once.

The incidentWhere, what and when, from a person or from any SI assistant that speaks MCP.
➜
hazbriefAsks every source at the same time. Combines the answers as they arrive. If a source fails, it says so and falls back.
➜
The pictureThe map, the cloud over time, the people, the responders, the briefing.
What it draws on
Census Bureau people, workplaces, places, roads National Weather Service the wind forecast NOAA radar and cloud Emergency Response Guidebook distances and first actions Federal hazmat regulations the materials table NOAA and EPA chemical database what each material does Medicare and Medicaid hospitals and nursing homes Federal maps schools, stations, rail, water Published gas models the cloud, grounded in the science
hazbrief10
Technical approach · key decisions

Five decisions that shaped it.

1
Use the accepted science. Never invent our own.
The gas models are published, open ones the field already knows. The chemistry of the release picks the model.
2
Show the gas over time.
A single fixed shape cannot tell a commander what to do next. Time is what planning needs.
3
Keep the person in the checking seat.
We assemble; the expert verifies. Guided alerts keep critical thinking engaged.
4
A source on every number.
Free public data, each value traceable to where it came from and when.
5
One server any SI assistant can use.
Built on the open MCP standard, so it is not tied to one vendor or one screen.
hazbrief11
Technical approach · why trust it

Every number shows its source. The testing is on the page.

  • A source on every number, one click away.
  • Every picture comes with its own test page, open to anyone.
  • Nobody can test on a live incident. So we use published benchmarks from field experiments to validate and verify the models.
  • Our yardsticks are HPAC and ALOHA, the accepted standards. The goal is statistical equivalence with them.
Benchmarked on a real chlorine release experiment, against the published results of HPAC and ALOHA.

Jack Rabbit II field trial. The full table of tests and results is in our evaluation write-up.

hazbrief12
Demonstration of functionality

The demonstration is live, from one start page.

  • Open a recorded run.A prepared scenario from our test set, exactly as it was recorded.
  • Run it with today's conditions.The same place and material, right now, on today's forecast.
  • Enter a new incident.A point on the map and one line about what happened.
  • The gas cloud plays as it is computed, and the briefing is ready to print.
hazbrief13
Beyond the incident

The same tool works before anything goes wrong.

PlanAbout 11,740 facilities file a worst-case release plan with the EPA, and every local emergency planning committee must plan for releases. Each one is a picture we can draw.
Ask "what if"Set the wind, the hour or the place and run it again. Day against night. Today's forecast against the worst case. This works today.
TrainPut a new responder in the chair with a realistic incident on their own roads, with no software to learn first.
RehearseTabletop exercises with a ready list of events: what the cloud reaches, and when, in time order.
hazbrief14
What is next

This is a working prototype. Here is where we take it.

  • Live traffic and traffic cameras around the scene
  • A real-time conversational assistant: ask the knowledge base, adjust the scenario, explore what-ifs
  • Smoke, fire and other hazards
  • More interactive, exploratory views of the picture
  • More field trials against the accepted standards
  • Design sessions with responders
Every minute counts. We give them back.
